Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Darkness: Dark spaces, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
Rajesh Patel is a sixty-one-year-old paramedic who has spent three decades responding to emergencies across the city. He is married, with grown children who live in other states, and until two years ago he thought he had seen everything. The call came on a humid October night—a tanker truck had overturned on the interstate, spilling an industrial solvent. The scene was chaotic: flashing lights, the sharp chemical bite in the air, and a driver trapped in the cab. Rajesh and his partner worked quickly, but as he helped extricate the driver, a valve on the tank released a burst of vapor. He inhaled before he could turn away. For a few seconds he could not breathe, his throat clamped shut, his eyes streaming. The taste—metallic and sweet, like cheap alcohol—stayed with him for days. He was decontaminated at the scene and sent home, told the exposure was brief and unlikely to cause lasting harm.

In the weeks that followed, Rajesh found himself unable to shake the feeling that he had somehow missed something, that the accident could have been prevented if he had checked the tank’s position more carefully. He began replaying the sequence in his mind, trying to spot the moment he should have acted differently. The rumination became a fixed habit—whenever there was a quiet moment on a shift or at home, his thoughts would drift back to that night. He started to dread stillness. At first, he simply turned on the television or picked up his phone. Soon, he began arranging his life so that he was never alone with his thoughts. He volunteered for every extra shift, accepted invitations from colleagues to grab coffee after work, and spent evenings on the phone with his brother or his grown daughter. His wife noticed that he seemed unable to sit through dinner without getting up to check something or to start a conversation that could stretch into the night. She assumed it was work stress and let it pass.

The real trouble came when the memories started to arrive without warning. A dimly lit hallway at the station—the backup generator was out once, and the darkness instantly brought back the hazy, smoke-filled interstate, his chest tightening as if the vapor were still in his lungs. He had to excuse himself and stand outside, breathing hard, his hands trembling. The same happened one evening at a family gathering when someone opened a bottle of whiskey. The faint alcohol smell hit him, and suddenly he was back in the truck cab, the sweet-metallic taste flooding his mouth. He could feel the terror—raw, physical, as though the event were happening again. His wife found him pale and sweating in the bathroom, and he lied, said he had eaten something bad.

The most difficult consequence was that he began avoiding the very places and situations that defined his profession. Hospitals became unbearable: the antiseptic smells, the busy corridors, the sight of an ambulance bay. He started calling in sick for shifts that involved hospital drop-offs, and he asked to be reassigned to light duty. When his supervisor pressed him about frequent sick leave, Rajesh said he was having trouble with his back. He avoided his annual physical—something he had never done before—and told himself he would reschedule later. The avoidance shrank his world. He stopped meeting his old crew for lunch because their talk inevitably turned to runs. He stopped walking past the garage where the rigs were stored. At home, he kept every light on at night. The darkness of the bedroom, even with a nightlight, made him feel trapped.

It was his wife who finally insisted he see someone. She had found him standing in the kitchen at 2 a.m., staring at nothing, a full cup of cold tea in his hand. He had not slept properly in months. What brought Rajesh to the clinic was not the terror itself but the exhaustion—the constant vigilance, the effort required to stay in the middle of a crowd, the hollow feeling that he was barely holding his life together. He wanted to stop being afraid of a smell. He wanted to drive an ambulance without his heart pounding. He wanted, more than anything, to be able to sit quietly in his own home and not have to run from his own mind.
